Dionysius of Heraclea, the tyrant, having been slender in his young years, became little by little so monstrously fat, paunchy and pot-bellied that he was constrained at night to apply a great quantity of leeches to his body, to suck out of him the excessive superfluity of the humour which made him so fat and corpulent. I leave aside Louis the Fat, thirty-ninth King of France, who flourished from the year 1110 to the year 1137, who became so immoderately big and fat that he carried away from it the surname of the Fat.

Still less can one allege the dissimilarity between the said accused and Sanxi Guerre, son of Martin: for besides that such judgments by resemblance (as has been often said above) are not very sure, there is a contrary summary inquiry upon the resemblance of the prisoner with the sisters of Martin Guerre, and one more probable, inasmuch as the likeness is with a greater number of persons, and such as are of like age, or very nearly, with him to whom the comparison is made.

The philosophers, Arithmeticians and Geometers, teach that the greater and the more proper the proportion and analogy is between two things, the better and the more fitting is the argument from the one to the other <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>: as, for example, between two learned and virtuous persons, or two powerful and robust ones, because there are far more sympathies than between two others, of whom the one would be virtuous and learned and the other vicious and unlearned, or the one strong and robust, the other feeble and weak.
